intro: Rome's noble families turned trees into status symbols the way they turned villas into galleries. Cardinal Scipione Borghese's gardener planted a grove of oriental planes in the 1600s that foresters now call the oldest living trees in the city; the Pamphilj and Mattei families each planted cedars of Lebanon nearby, one per hilltop garden, as a shorthand for permanence. Rome has 65 trees registered as monumental under Italian law, more than any other city in the country. These twenty-two range from a poet's legendary oak to a South American ombu, and all but two are free to visit.
meta_description: Rome's noble villas planted cedars of Lebanon as status symbols. Meet Adonis, a 425-year-old plane in Villa Borghese, and twenty-three more remarkable trees.
question_answer: The oldest verified tree in Rome is Adonis, an oriental plane in the Valley of the Plane Trees at Villa Borghese, planted in the early 1600s by Cardinal Scipione Borghese's gardener and now around 425 years old. It stands inside Villa Borghese, a short walk from the Via Pinciana entrance.
question_meta: Adonis, a 425-year-old oriental plane in Villa Borghese, is Rome's oldest verified tree. Its story, exact location, and twenty-three more remarkable trees.
question_context: Rome has an older legend. The Quercia del Tasso on the Gianicolo is popularly said to be a thousand years old, tied to the poet Torquato Tasso, who tradition says rested in its shade before his death in 1595. No dendrologist has ever dated it, and this site treats that number as folklore rather than fact. Adonis has no such problem. Cardinal Scipione Borghese's gardener, Domenico Savini da Montepulciano, planted a row of oriental planes in the villa's private hunting park in the early 1600s, and the planting is documented well enough that Italian foresters count the survivors, nine of the original eleven, as the oldest confirmed trees in the city. Adonis is the largest of them, a hollow giant at the entrance to what is now called the Valley of the Plane Trees. In 2021 the garden cloned it from a single surviving leaf, a hedge against the fate of a neighboring oak from the same era that collapsed in 2018. Getting there: enter Villa Borghese from Via Pinciana and follow the signs for the Valle dei Platani.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Rome?
faq.a: Adonis, a 425-year-old oriental plane in Villa Borghese, is the oldest tree in Rome with a documented planting date. An older oak on the Gianicolo is popularly said to be a thousand years old, but no scientific dating backs the claim.

faq.q: Why does Rome have so many cedars of Lebanon?
faq.a: Roman noble families used them as garden status symbols from the 1600s onward. Villa Doria Pamphilj and Villa Celimontana each planted their own, prizing the species for its biblical associations with endurance and permanence.

faq.q: Are Rome's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Twenty of the twenty-two on this list stand in free public parks and squares. The two inside the Orto Botanico, Rome's botanical garden, require a paid ticket.

faq.q: How does Italy protect its monumental trees?
faq.a: A 2013 national law lets municipalities register trees of exceptional age, size or historical value as monumental. Rome has 65 of them, more than any other Italian city.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Villa Sciarra

location.address: Villa Sciarra, Viale Adolfo Leducq, 00153 Roma

trees.story: Rome's most famous old trees are cedars and planes, planted by cardinals and popes on grand estates. This ginkgo belongs to a very different Roman: George Washington Wurts, an American diplomat who bought this hillside property in 1902 and spent the rest of his life filling it with plants gathered from wherever caught his interest. He had the ginkgo planted in the early 1900s, one of the first established in the city, a species Europe had only known for about two centuries at that point, brought over from temple gardens in China where it had grown essentially unchanged since before the dinosaurs went extinct. Rome's own environment department now lists it among the city's roughly twenty official monumental trees, qualifying on three separate grounds at once: age and size, landscape value, and simple botanical rarity, since ginkgos remain genuinely uncommon in Roman parks even a century after Wurts planted his. The trunk has thickened to just over three metres around and the crown now reaches 25 metres, taller than most of the villa's own follies and fake ruins built around the same period. Wurts died in 1928 without seeing what came next: his widow, the American heiress Henrietta Tower Wurts, gave the whole seven and a half hectare estate to the Italian state in the early 1930s, on condition it stay a public park. Every November the tree does what ginkgos do everywhere, turning uniformly gold within days rather than fading gradually like its neighbours.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Sciarra public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Trastevere, or bus routes to Via Dandolo / Via Calandrelli

best_time.label: November, when it turns uniformly gold within days

trees.name: Adonis

location.address: Valle dei Platani, Villa Borghese, 00197 Roma

trees.story: Nine trees are what remain of the eleven Cardinal Scipione Borghese planted here four centuries ago. Adonis is the largest survivor: a vast, hollow-trunked oriental plane at the entrance to what is now called the Valley of the Plane Trees, planted in the early 1600s by the cardinal's gardener, Domenico Savini da Montepulciano. At around 425 years old, it and its siblings are described by Italian foresters as the only urban stand of ancient oriental planes left in the West, and the oldest living trees in Rome. In 2021 the garden cloned it, growing a sapling from a single leaf found sprouting on the fragile trunk. The clone, planted nearby as Adonis Junior, is genetically identical to a four-hundred-year-old tree despite being six years old at planting. It was a hedge against the inevitable: Adonis is hollow and propped, and a nearby oak from the same era, nicknamed the Quercia del Lupo for a wolf-shaped burl on its trunk and already documented in a memoir of the villa's gardens by the 1650s, collapsed in a storm in 2018 after three to five hundred years standing, accounts differ. Adonis is still leafing out every spring in the hunting park a cardinal built long before anyone thought to call it a public garden.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Borghese
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Metro A Spagna, entering via Via Pinciana
trees.notes: Coordinates now come from Italy's national monumental tree registry (MASAF), which lists a single individually-catalogued Platanus orientalis at this exact site (Villa Borghese, Valle dei Platani), matching Adonis's description as the grove's one officially registered specimen; moved from a park-wide estimate to this registry point, about 290m away. The registry's own growth-based estimate gives 407 years against the 425 cited elsewhere, the same order of disagreement already carried openly on rom_005 and rom_006, so the age range here is left as is rather than resolved. Photo (2009, Patafisik) downloaded and viewed directly 2026-07-27: shows a large oriental plane with a prominent hollow cavity in its trunk, standing among several similarly aged planes in a grassy grove, an unusually strong match to Adonis's own described hollow trunk and grove setting. The file's own caption does not name Adonis specifically among the grove's nine survivors, so approved as an honest illustration of the tree and its grove rather than a certain single-specimen match, the same standard used elsewhere on this project for ensemble scenes.

trees.name: The Twin Planes of the Eleven Fountains

location.address: Orto Botanico di Roma, Largo Cristina di Svezia 24, 00165 Roma
location.neighbourhood: Trastevere, at the foot of the Gianicolo

trees.story: Two oriental planes here are older than the university that now owns them. Rome's Botanical Garden became a state institution in 1883, but the ground itself was a private garden of the Corsini family from 1660 onward, and these two trees, flanking Ferdinando Fuga's 1742 cascade of eleven fountains, were already mature when the last Corsini cardinals walked past them. Foresters place their age at over 300 years, among the oldest confirmed trees in Rome after Villa Borghese's plane grove. The staircase they frame, the Scalinata delle Undici Fontane, sends water down five stone basins toward eleven separate jets, an 18th-century flourish built as a backdrop for planting that already existed. The garden today holds 345 centuries-old specimens across 130 species, cork oaks, Himalayan cedars and Turkish oaks among them, but the two planes at the fountains remain the postcard image, framing water and stone the way they have for three centuries, regardless of which family or which state held the deed to the land around them.
trees.access: Paid entry, Orto Botanico di Roma
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Trastevere (Piazza Trilussa), or tram 8 to Piazza Sonnino
trees.notes: Two trees described as one entry, matching how the garden itself presents them (a pair flanking the staircase). Age range is a general foresters' estimate; no source gives an exact planting year for either specimen. Photo viewed directly: shows the monumental staircase at the Fontana degli Undici Zampilli flanked by two large trees with gnarled branches and mottled bark, an unambiguous match to the story's own description.

trees.name: The Cork Oak of the Orangery

location.address: Orto Botanico di Roma, near the Orangery, Largo Cristina di Svezia 24, 00165 Roma
location.neighbourhood: Trastevere, at the foot of the Gianicolo

trees.story: This cork oak has been measured twice in three years, and it grew in the interval: 5.00 meters around in October 2021, 5.30 meters by January 2024, still adding girth at an age Italy's national monumental tree registry puts at 226 years. It grows near the Orangery in Rome's Botanical Garden, one of several cork oaks the university lists among its monumental specimens, alongside Turkish oaks and a pair of Himalayan cedars near the old riding school. Quercus suber is farmed across the western Mediterranean for its bark, stripped every decade or so to make wine corks and flooring without killing the tree, and this specimen's deeply fissured, spongy trunk still shows the scars of past harvests even though nobody has stripped it in living memory. It predates the garden's official 1883 founding as a state institution by nearly a century, rooted here since the grounds still belonged to the Corsini family. Visitors tend to walk straight past it toward the garden's showier Japanese section and its cascading fountains, but few trees anywhere in the city are still visibly getting bigger.
trees.access: Paid entry, Orto Botanico di Roma
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Trastevere (Piazza Trilussa), or tram 8 to Piazza Sonnino

trees.name: The Cedar of the Belvedere

location.address: Belvedere del Lago del Giglio, Villa Doria Pamphilj, Via Aurelia Antica, 00165 Roma

trees.story: Sources disagree by a century and a half on how old this cedar is, and the disagreement is the most honest thing anyone can say about it. One detailed study of Villa Doria Pamphilj's tree collection places its planting in the 1600s, when the Pamphilj family first laid out the estate, which would make it over 300 years old. The tree's own entry in Italy's national monumental tree registry gives a calculated age closer to 150 years, with a trunk 4.6 meters around and a height of 30 meters. Both figures describe the same cedar, shading the belvedere terrace above the Lago del Giglio in Rome's largest public park. What is not disputed is the setting: Villa Doria Pamphilj was a private hunting and pleasure ground until the Italian state expropriated it in 1965, and this cedar, whichever planting it dates to, has shaded cardinals, princes and now Sunday joggers from the same terrace above the same ornamental lake. It is listed as the only individually registered monumental tree in a park that otherwise counts its history in family names rather than tree ages.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Doria Pamphilj
trees.transport: Bus 870 or 791 to the Via Aurelia Antica entrance, 10 min walk
trees.notes: Age disputed between two sources by up to 170 years (17th-century planting theory vs. a 150-year registry estimate); the expropriation year (1965) is given by secondary sources and should be checked against a primary record. Pin corrected 2026-07-26, a real correction of about 1.2km, not just imprecision: two Wiki Loves Monuments Italia photos independently titled "Cedro del Libano" at Villa Doria Pamphilj (by different photographers, 2021 and a companion shot from the lake canal) carry identical embedded GPS at 41.882956, 12.444775, which also matches Italy's national monumental tree registry (MASAF, AMI code 27/H501/RM/12, locality "Villa Pamphili - Belvedere del Lago del Giglio") to the hundredth of an arcsecond, byte-identical across two separate spreadsheet fetches. The previous pin was roughly 1.2km away, closer to the Via Aurelia Antica entrance than to the Belvedere itself. Photo downloaded and viewed directly 2026-07-27: close-up of blue-green needle clusters and upright barrel cones unmistakably Cedrus libani, consistent with the file's own title and the confirmed GPS. Approved.

trees.name: The Leccio of the Lake

location.address: Viale del Lago, Villa Borghese, 00197 Roma

trees.story: Marcantonio IV Borghese tore out six hundred holm oaks in 1784 to build an English-style garden around Villa Borghese's lake, and one tree, by luck or design, was left standing. This is that leccio, growing at the water's edge in what locals once called the Piano dei Licini, the holm oak plain, before the prince's landscapers decided a lake and a temple suited fashionable taste better than a forest. Italy's national tree registry measures its trunk at 4.3 meters around and calculates an age of 176 years from growth data, a figure that would place its planting after Borghese's makeover rather than before it. Older estimates, based on the site's documented history rather than direct measurement, put it closer to 300, arguing it is one of the few survivors of the original grove. Both cannot be right. This page gives both rather than pick a side. What both agree on is the tree's stature: 19 meters tall, its dense evergreen crown reflected in the artificial lake that replaced six hundred of its relatives two and a half centuries ago.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Borghese
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Metro A Spagna, via the Giardino del Lago
trees.notes: Age genuinely disputed: the national registry's measured estimate (176 years) contradicts the traditional account (up to 300 years, tied to the 1784 garden redesign). Presented as a range rather than resolved.

trees.name: The Cedar of the Garibaldi Mausoleum

location.address: Via Giuseppe Garibaldi 29, Gianicolo, 00153 Roma

trees.story: This cedar shares its hillside with the dead of a revolution. It grows between the Fontana dell'Acqua Paola and the Mausoleo Ossario Garibaldino, the 1941 monument holding the remains of those killed defending Rome's short-lived Republic in 1849 and fighting to make the city Italy's capital between 1860 and 1870. Officially measured for the national monumental tree registry, it stands about 20 meters tall with a trunk 5.74 meters around, and its documented age of roughly 146 years puts its planting in the 1870s, soon after Rome became the capital of a unified Italy in 1871 and this hillside turned from battlefield into a place of civic memory. Cedars of Lebanon are not native anywhere near the Gianicolo; Roman nobility, and later the new Italian state, planted them across the city's hilltop gardens as a shorthand for permanence and old-world grandeur, the same reasoning that put cedars in half the noble villas on this list. This one has outlasted the reasoning: nobody plants status symbols on a war memorial today, but the tree stayed, and it is now the memorial's oldest living feature.
trees.access: Free, open access, Gianicolo
trees.transport: Bus 115 or 870 to Gianicolo, short walk

trees.name: The Cedar of Celimontana

location.address: Viale Cardinale Francesco Spellman, Villa Celimontana, 00184 Roma

trees.story: A few meters from Villa Celimontana's Aleppo pine grows its opposite in almost every way: straight where the pine leans, dense and dark where the pine is sparse, native to a mountain range a thousand kilometers further east. This cedar of Lebanon is one of two of Rome's officially monumental trees inside the villa, both standing along Viale Cardinale Francesco Spellman near the main entrance at Piazza della Navicella. Ciriaco Mattei began turning the site's vineyards into an ornamental garden in 1572, and cedars of Lebanon, prized in noble Roman gardens for their biblical associations with endurance, show up across the city's hilltop villas from the 1600s onward. No record fixes the year this particular tree went into the ground, only its registry status as a monumental specimen for its age, dimensions and form, so this account treats its age as undocumented rather than claim a number it cannot back. The villa passed to the Italian Geographical Society in 1926 and became public parkland in 1928, and the cedar, whatever its exact age, has outlasted every institution that has owned the ground beneath it.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Celimontana
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Metro B Colosseo, via Piazza della Navicella
trees.notes: No source gives a planting date or age figure; the municipal registry designates it monumental without a number. Age range here is a conservative placeholder, not a sourced estimate. Pin corrected 2026-07-26: the already-approved photo's own embedded GPS (41.885192, 12.494350) places this named, identified cedar precisely; a second independent Commons photo of the same named tree by a different photographer (Albarubescens, 2019) carries an almost identical GPS reading, and a third (Piroetta, 2021) lands about 26m away, consistent with the same tree. Also cross-checked against the neighbouring Aleppo pine's (rom_009) MASAF registry point, about 20-25m away, matching this story's "a few meters apart" framing.

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine of Celimontana

location.address: Viale Cardinale Francesco Spellman, Villa Celimontana, 00184 Roma

trees.story: Villa Celimontana keeps two of Rome's officially monumental trees within a few meters of each other, and this Aleppo pine is the more unusual of the pair. Pinus halepensis is a Mediterranean coastal species, more at home on the cliffs above Aleppo or along the Ligurian shore than on the Caelian Hill, and its presence here fits the exotic-planting habit of the Mattei family, who turned a vineyard into this garden starting in 1572. The tree stands along Viale Cardinale Francesco Spellman near the villa's main entrance at Piazza della Navicella, its twisting, wind-shaped canopy a contrast to the straighter cedar growing almost beside it. No source gives the pine a precise planting date, only the national registry's designation as monumental for its age, dimensions and form, so this account states it as undocumented rather than invent a number. What is certain is the company it has kept: Renaissance nobles, then the Italian Geographical Society, which held the villa from 1926, and now Sunday footballers on the grounds nearby, all under the same slanted pine.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Celimontana
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Metro B Colosseo, via Piazza della Navicella
trees.notes: No source gives a planting date or age figure; the municipal registry designates it monumental without a number. Age range here is a conservative placeholder, not a sourced estimate. Coordinates now come from Italy's national monumental tree registry (MASAF), the only Pinus halepensis entry at this Viale Cardinale Spellman site, about 210m from the previous general estimate.

trees.name: The Fitolacca of the Capitoline

location.address: Piazza d'Aracoeli, at the Cordonata, Campidoglio, 00186 Roma

trees.story: Rome's most improbable street tree is originally from the Argentine pampas, and it owes its spot on the Capitoline Hill to a 50th birthday party. Prince Baldassarre Ladislao Odescalchi planted it in 1911, the year Italy marked half a century since unification, at the foot of Michelangelo's Cordonata staircase beside the church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli. It is a Phytolacca dioica, called ombu in its native South America, a fast-growing evergreen with a swollen, buttressed trunk that looks more sculpted than grown. At roughly 115 years old it is the youngest tree on this list by a wide margin, but nothing else on the Capitoline canopy touches its scale: its crown now shades a stretch of the climb toward Piazza del Campidoglio, competing for attention with the ancient temple platform the hill was named for. Tourists photograph the she-wolf statue and the Michelangelo-designed piazza above; the tree that actually shades their walk up rarely gets a caption. It is one of Rome's officially registered monumental trees despite being, in local terms, barely out of its youth.
trees.access: Free, public steps, always accessible
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Piazza Venezia

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the German Institute

location.address: Villa Sciarra, Istituto Italiano di Studi Germanici, Via Calandrelli 25, 00153 Roma

trees.story: Two official registers disagree about this trunk by nearly two metres. Italy's national list gives it as five metres around; the Lazio regional list, which is where the national one gets its Roman entries in the first place, says 3.3. Both are describing the same deodar standing beside the villa's main house, and neither has ever put a date on it. What the regional list does say is unusual: of the 65 monumental trees inside the comune of Roma, this is one of only three designated partly for architettura vegetale, vegetal architecture, the surveyor's term for a tree whose shape is itself the built object. Not its age. Not its girth. Its form. Cedrus deodara grows wild at 1,500 to 3,000 metres in the western Himalaya, where its Sanskrit name means timber of the gods and its wood built temples. This one arrived by way of a rich American's shopping habit. George Washington Wurts bought the hillside in 1902 and spent 26 years filling it with plants from wherever caught his attention, the ginkgo 130 metres downhill among them. The house behind the cedar became the Italian Institute of German Studies in 1931, three years after Wurts died, and the tree has been institutional property ever since.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Sciarra public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Trastevere, or bus to Via Dandolo / Via Calandrelli
trees.notes: Sheet 10/H501/RM/12. Existence, species and location confirmed by three sources (Lazio regional register, Roma Capitale's own monumental-tree page, abitarearoma.it). No source anywhere gives an age or planting date, so the range here is a conservative placeholder tied to the Wurts era (1902-1928), not a sourced estimate, exactly as on rom_008 and rom_009. Girth genuinely disputed between the two registers: MASAF national 500cm, Lazio regional 330cm, same sheet number and same coordinates. Height agrees at 20m. The story states the disagreement rather than picking one. Coordinates are the register's own GPS, identical in both lists; converted from the regional list's DMS (41 deg 53' 00,19", 12 deg 27' 53,03") they match the national decimal figure. 130m from rom_001.

trees.name: The Podocarp of Villa Sciarra

location.address: Viale Adolfo Leducq, Villa Sciarra, 00153 Roma

trees.story: Most trees earn a place on Italy's monumental register for being old or enormous. This one is on it for being strange. The Lazio survey gives its reason as a single letter, d, botanical rarity, and lists no other qualifying criterion at all: not age, not size, not landscape value. At two metres around and 18 metres tall it is a decent tree in a city full of far bigger ones, and the state protects it anyway, because there is essentially nothing else like it growing in Rome. Podocarps are a mostly southern conifer family that split off long before pines existed and never adopted the cone. Instead the seed sits on a swollen fleshy stalk that turns purple and gets eaten by birds, which is why Podocarpus neriifolius spread from the Himalayan foothills to New Guinea and why Buddhist communities planted it around temples across that whole range. Rome's own city government calls this specimen splendid and enormous. It stands on Viale Adolfo Leducq roughly 20 metres from the ginkgo, both of them bought by the same American collector in the same decade, which makes this stretch of path the most botanically improbable 50 metres in the city.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Sciarra public park
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Trastevere, or bus to Via Dandolo / Via Calandrelli
trees.notes: Sheet 09/H501/RM/12, 200cm girth, 18m, both registers agreeing. Sole monumentality criterion in the Lazio list is 'd) rarita botanica', which is the story's opening claim and is quoted from the register itself. No age or planting date exists in any source; range is a placeholder tied to the Wurts era, not an estimate. abitarearoma.it independently describes it as 'un raro esemplare di Podocarpo (il pino con cui i buddisti ornavano i loro templi)' and Roma Capitale's page as a 'splendid and enormous' specimen. Common name: no other city file uses Podocarpus, so 'Willowleaf Podocarp' is chosen as the nationality-neutral name per hard rule 9; if a later Podocarpus ships elsewhere it must match this. 20m from rom_001.

trees.name: The Plane of Piazza San Cosimato

location.address: Piazza di San Cosimato, play area, 00153 Roma

trees.story: The neighbourhood had this tree scanned. Volunteers in Trastevere paid forest agronomists to run a tomography on the trunk, reading the internal soundness of the wood the way a hospital reads a body, because the tree stands directly over the square's children's play area and nobody wanted to guess. At 5.65 metres around it holds the thickest plane trunk on Rome's monumental register, thicker than the celebrated planes of Villa Borghese, and it grows not in a cardinal's garden but in a working piazza with a morning market, a football pitch's worth of parked scooters and a tenth-century church. The square was open pasture until the 1880s, the Prati di San Cosimato, grazing land outside the tight medieval lanes. When Rome became the capital and Trastevere was rebuilt, the fields became a triangular market square, and the plane either survived that or was planted into it; no document says which, and its 2013 addition to the register recorded size without age. Platanus x acerifolia is itself an accident, an eighteenth-century hybrid of the eastern and American planes that turned out to tolerate city air better than either parent. Rome planted thousands. This is the one the neighbours look after.
trees.access: Free, public square, always accessible
trees.transport: Tram 8 to Piazza Sonnino, then 5 min walk; 10 min walk from Piazza Trilussa
trees.notes: Sheet 57/H501/RM/12, 565cm, 20m, locality given as 'Piazza San Cosimato area ludica' (the play area), which is what fixes the pin to one obvious tree in a small square. Second source is Il Messaggero's report on the neighbourhood's adoption of the tree and the stability tomography, independent of the register; archidiap's architectural study of the piazza corroborates the play area under a 'platano secolare' and the 1880s reshaping of the square. No age published anywhere. Superlative checked (hard rule 8): 565cm is the largest single plane girth among the 65 Roma register entries, ahead of Viale Jonio at 553cm; the Valle dei Platani and Fontane Oscure figures are group maxima for a different species, Platanus orientalis, so the claim is limited to plane trunks on the register and states its bounds. Bridges the Villa Sciarra walk to the Orto Botanico walk: 700m from rom_001, 600m from rom_003.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Cordonata

location.address: Via delle Tre Pile, Campidoglio, 00186 Roma

trees.story: A Balkan mountain tree has no business being this large on a Roman hill. Aesculus hippocastanum grows wild in a handful of ravines in the mountains of northern Greece, Albania and North Macedonia, where the summers are cool and the soil stays damp; western Europe only met it in the 1500s, through Constantinople, and planted it everywhere as an avenue tree. Rome is close to the edge of what it tolerates, which is why the city has exactly one on its monumental register and why a trunk 3.45 metres around here counts for more than the same figure would in Vienna. It stands on Via delle Tre Pile, the ramp cars take up the Capitoline, on the right-hand side of Michelangelo's Cordonata as you climb. Roma Capitale registered it for size and for landscape value, meaning the view it belongs to rather than the tree alone. Almost everyone who photographs the staircase stands in its shade to do it. Fifty metres away on the other flank of the same climb grows the ombu from Argentina, so the two flanks of Rome's most famous stair are held by a Balkan mountain tree and a South American pampas tree, and neither is Roman at all.
trees.access: Free, public street, always accessible
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Piazza Venezia, up Via delle Tre Pile

best_time.label: late September, when the conkers start dropping onto the ramp

trees.notes: Sheet 01/H501/RM/12, 345cm, 20m, criteria a) age/size and f) landscape value. Roma Capitale's own monumental-tree page names it independently and places it on the right of the Cordonata on via delle Tre Pile, which is the second source for existence and location. No age published; range is a placeholder, not an estimate. Pin: the register's DMS (41 deg 53' 36,25", 12 deg 28' 55,88") converts to the national list's decimal figure exactly, and two Wiki Loves Monuments Italia photographs by different contributors carry embedded GPS identical to it, so the position is independently confirmed rather than register-only. Photo downloaded at 960px and viewed directly 2026-08-05: a big horse chestnut in full green leaf against blue sky, daylight, in colour, filling the left two thirds of the frame with the Capitoline balustrade behind and a cypress at the right edge; the centre band of the image is canopy, so it survives the wide card crop. Trunk is not visible (the shot looks up from the ramp), which is the one departure from the Cadiz standard; approved anyway as the best of eight candidates, the alternatives being more distant views with the Vittoriano dominating. Only Aesculus on Rome's register. best_time set to fruit rather than the April flower candles deliberately: September is one of the two thinnest months on the season shelf and the conkers on a public stair are the more useful reason to go.

trees.name: The Cedar Above the Lake

location.address: Viale del Lago, Giardino del Lago, Villa Borghese, 00197 Roma

trees.story: Rome's own list of monumental trees does not describe this cedar on its own. It describes it as accompanied by a monumental holm oak, and the two really do stand 70 metres apart at the same water. That phrasing is the giveaway: this tree was never meant to be looked at as a specimen. When Marcantonio IV Borghese remade the grounds in the 1780s he was buying a painting, not a collection. His architects Antonio and Mario Asprucci dug an artificial lake, put an island in it, built a small Ionic temple to Aesculapius on the island in 1786, and planted around all of it to make the view from the bank look like a landscape that had always been there. The cedar is scenery, and it is doing the job two and a half centuries later: 4.1 metres around, 22 metres tall, a flat candelabra crown leaning out over the rowing boats. Cedrus libani was the prestige tree of that generation of Roman gardens, planted in half the noble villas on this list, but most of those sit on lawns and terraces. This one has water under it, which is why it is the one people photograph.
trees.access: Free, open access, Villa Borghese
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Metro A Spagna, via the Giardino del Lago
trees.notes: Sheet 22/H501/RM/12, 410cm, 22m. Roma Capitale's monumental-tree page names it independently and explicitly pairs it with the monumental holm oak, which is our rom_006, 70m away; that pairing is the second source and also the reason this entry exists, since it thickens an existing walk rather than adding a lonely point. No age published anywhere. The 120-200 range is a placeholder consistent with the growth-based figures the national registry calculates for comparable Roman cedars (146 years at 574cm on rom_007, about 150 at 460cm on rom_005), and the story does not state a number. Pin independently confirmed: three Commons photographs by the same Wiki Loves Monuments contributor, taken 2018, 2020 and 2022, all carry embedded GPS identical to the register coordinate to six decimals. Photo (2022) downloaded at 960px and viewed directly 2026-08-05: the whole tree in summer daylight, in colour, filling the frame above the lake basin and its iron railing, trunk and candelabra crown both readable, centre band all tree. A clean Cadiz-standard match. The 2020 file by the same author was rejected: it is a close-up of trunk and branches only. Temple of Aesculapius date (1786) and the Asprucci attribution come from the villa's standard history, not from the register.

trees.name: The Redwood of the Pincio

location.address: Pincio, Villa Borghese, 00187 Roma

trees.story: Thirty metres is a good height for a tree in Rome and a failure for this species. Sequoia sempervirens is the tallest living thing on earth, passing 110 metres in the fog belt of northern California, and it gets there by drinking the fog directly through its leaves during a rainless summer. Rome offers it a rainless summer without the fog. So the redwood on the Pincio has grown thick instead of tall, 4.2 metres around, and still ends up among the five tallest trees on the city's entire monumental register, which says more about Rome's trees than about this one. It grows on Giuseppe Valadier's terrace, laid out between 1809 and 1814 during the French occupation as a public promenade above Piazza del Popolo, at a moment when Roman gardening was swinging from clipped geometry to imported curiosities. Nobody has published when it was planted or by whom. It reached the national register late, in the batch of Roman trees added after the well-documented ones, and that entry is the only document about it that exists: species, girth, height, a coordinate. Everything else anyone tells you about this tree is a guess, including the ones that sound confident.
trees.access: Free, open access, Pincio gardens
trees.transport: 10 min walk up the ramps from Piazza del Popolo, or Metro A Flaminio
trees.notes: Sheet 68/H501/RM/12, 420cm, 30m. SINGLE SOURCE, and the story says so in its last three sentences rather than hiding it: the Lazio regional register and the MASAF national register are the same designation published twice, and no municipal, press or garden-history source names this individual tree. Roma Capitale's own monumental-tree walk predates the sheets numbered above 57 and does not cover it. Published under the flagged rule because the register is an official source and the uncertainty is stated on the page; drop it if a reader disputes the tree. Superlative checked (hard rule 8): NOT the tallest on the register. Rome's register tops out at 34m (the Aleppo pine at Villa Celimontana, our rom_009), then 32m twice, then 31m, then this at 30m, so the claim is written as among the five tallest and is arithmetically true of the 65 comune entries. Precision is approximate, not confirmed: the Pincio terrace is large, the coordinate has no independent corroboration (no Commons photograph of this tree exists, geosearch and text search both empty), and the Caserta lesson says a register point with nothing to check it against is not a confirmed pin. 470m from rom_006, so it extends the Villa Borghese walk toward Piazza del Popolo rather than starting a new one.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Via Corsini

location.address: Via Corsini 1, 00165 Roma

trees.access: Free, public street (Via Corsini), RAMI records it as Accessibile. Resolves the access question the leads file left open: it stands on the street at Via Corsini 1, not inside the ticketed Orto Botanico or the private Corsini gardens.
trees.transport: Same walk as rom_003 (Twin Planes of the Eleven Fountains), 109m away; 10 min walk from Trastevere
trees.story:
Rome's oldest magnolia does not stand in a garden. It stands on the pavement of Via Corsini, outside the wall of the palace whose garden it was planted for, around the middle of the eighteenth century and roughly 275 years ago. The Orto Botanico next door, the obvious home for a tree like this, only became a public institution long after it was already in the ground.

Southern magnolias had reached Europe from the American southeast only a few decades earlier, which made this one a collector's purchase rather than a street tree. It grew accordingly. The trunk measures 290 centimetres around and the crown reaches 18 metres, closer to a forest tree than to the clipped courtyard shrub the species usually settles for in Italy. Italy's monumental register lists it for age and for size, and for a magnolia that pairing is rare.

What it has watched is mostly the boundary in front of it changing hands: a cardinal's private grounds turning into a state botanical collection, and Trastevere turning from the edge of the city into the middle of it. Surveyors looked it over in late 2025 and recorded its health as good.

In May and June it does the thing the species was imported for, opening cream-white flowers the size of a spread hand, high up and out of reach, and heavy enough with scent that most people smell it before they look up.

best_time.label: May and June, when the cream-white flowers open and you smell it before you see it

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Villa Torlonia

location.address: Villa Torlonia, entrance staircase to the Palazzo Nobile (Casino Nobile), Via Nomentana, 00161 Roma

trees.access: Free, public park, Villa Torlonia. RAMI records it as Accessibile.
trees.transport: Bus to Via Nomentana / Villa Torlonia entrance, or 10 min walk from Bologna metro (Line B); 3.5km from the city centre
trees.story:
No cedar on Rome's monumental register is thicker than this one. Six metres around the trunk, 28 metres up, standing beside the staircase Giuseppe Valadier designed for the Casino Nobile. The surveyor who wrote its entry reached for the word guardiano.

Nobody knows when it was planted, and that is worth saying plainly, because the register carries a girth for it and no birth year at all. What exists instead is the estate's history. The Torlonia family bought the grounds in 1797, and the English-style landscaping that brought ornamental conifers into Roman villas came later in the nineteenth century. That puts the cedar somewhere between 150 and 220 years old, which is an inference from the garden rather than a date from a document.

Its neighbours have been unusual. The park holds a pink granite obelisk the cedar now rivals for height, a mock-medieval house covered in owls, and from 1925 to 1943 Mussolini, who rented the whole estate as his private residence for a token sum. The villa was occupied, then left to fall apart for decades, then repaired and opened as a public park. The cedar came through all of it standing where it stands now. Roma Capitale's own description of the villa calls it colossal, which for once is not municipal enthusiasm. It was measured again in March 2026 and found in good health.

trees.name: The Podocarp of Piazza Vittorio

location.address: Giardino Nicola Calipari, Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II, 00185 Roma

trees.access: Free, public garden inside Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II (Giardino Nicola Calipari). RAMI records it as Accessibile.
trees.transport: Vittorio Emanuele metro (Line A), on the square; 1.7km from the Capitoline cluster (rom_010, rom_014)
trees.story:
Italy put this tree on its national monumental register in October 2025 for one reason: it should not be here. Podocarpus neriifolius grows wild in the forests of the Himalayan foothills and southeast Asia, and Rome holds very few of any size. This is one of the largest, 230 centimetres around and 20 metres tall, in the public garden inside Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II.

Its age is not known. No planting record survives and neither register that lists it carries a date, so a century, give or take, is as precise as anyone can honestly be. The square around it was laid out in the 1880s for the new capital's civil servants, in an arcaded Turinese style that still makes this corner of Rome look imported from somewhere else, and a garden of exotic trees was exactly what that decade planted.

It has stood through the more restless version of Rome. The square's ruined fountain, the Trofei di Mario, sits a few steps away and predates it by seventeen centuries. The food market that filled the arcades for a hundred years packed up and moved around the corner in 2001. The neighbourhood became the most polyglot in the city. The podocarp, evergreen and unbothered, looks much the same in February as in August. Its health was recorded as good in November 2025.

trees.name: The Chir Pine of Colle Oppio
trees.age_estimate: 90+ years, likely planted around the garden's 1936 opening

location.address: Parco di Colle Oppio, above the Domus Aurea, 00184 Roma

trees.access: Free, public park, Parco di Colle Oppio. RAMI records it as Accessibile.
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Colosseo metro (Line B); joins a future Celio/Colosseum walk, 1km from Villa Celimontana (rom_008, rom_009)
trees.story:
The roots of this pine have grown into Nero's palace. It stands on Colle Oppio directly above the Domus Aurea, and somewhere below it in the dark they have worked into the nymphaeum of Ulysses and Polyphemus.

It is not a Roman tree in any sense. The Chir Pine belongs to the Himalayan foothills, and this one was carried back from there by Giuseppe Tucci, the Tibetologist and Mussolini-era envoy who spent the 1930s travelling in Tibet and Nepal. It was already standing when the Colle Oppio garden was inaugurated in 1936, which makes it at least ninety years old and one of the very few of its species in the city. Italy's monumental register added it in October 2025 on the grounds of botanical rarity alone: 290 centimetres around, 20 metres tall.

The caveat is real and belongs in the same breath. Those roots are a genuine problem for the ruin underneath, and plans to redesign the garden above the Domus Aurea have been reported as intending to take out the tall trees over the excavation for exactly that reason. The press had already written this tree off as dying once. The register's most recent check, in late 2025, found it alive and in good health. Both things hold: it is doing well, and it is standing on ground where the archaeology has the stronger claim.

trees.name: The Cypress of Piazza di Siena

location.address: Piazza di Siena perimeter, Villa Borghese

trees.story: Eighteen cypresses once ringed Piazza di Siena when the arena was laid out in 1789, part of the original hedge and tree enclosure designed by architect Antonio Asprucci for what is now Rome's international horse show. Seventeen of those eighteen are gone. This one, according to the conservation group Amici di Villa Borghese, is the sole survivor, still standing along the same oval perimeter the arena has kept since the eighteenth century. Rome's own municipal history of the piazza confirms the original planting scheme, a boxwood hedge, eighteen cypresses and two pine groves, without naming which tree is the last of the batch, so the survivor claim rests on the advocacy group's word rather than a dendrologist's ring count. What isn't in dispute is the arena itself: it has hosted the Concorso Ippico Internazionale, Rome's showjumping event, every year since 1922, riders and horses circling the same green oval a two centuries old cypress has watched from the sidelines the whole time. The letter naming this tree was written in 2024 because Villa Borghese was losing historic specimens faster than anyone wanted, including a well loved pine on the nearby Pincio that was felled around the same period. This cypress is what the campaign wanted people to notice before it went the same way.
trees.access: Free, public park, walkway around the Piazza di Siena arena
trees.transport: Roughly 10-15 min walk from Spagna or Flaminio metro (Line A), inside Villa Borghese
trees.notes: The 'sole survivor of the 1789 planting' claim rests on a single advocacy letter (Amici di Villa Borghese, carteinregola.it, 2024), corroborated only for the general historical fact (18 cypresses planted 1789) by Rome's own municipal history page, not for which specific tree survived. Pin is the piazza's centre, not the individual tree, since no source identifies which cypress along the perimeter is the 1789 survivor.

trees.name: The Hackberries of the Aranciera
trees.age_estimate: locally described as dating from the 1600s, no dendrological confirmation

location.address: Holm oak grove (Lecceta) between the Aranciera / Museo Carlo Bilotti and the Muro Torto, Villa Borghese

trees.story: A hackberry in the holm oak wood behind the Museo Carlo Bilotti carries a nickname rather than a certificate: locals call it il bagolaro del Seicento, the hackberry of the 1600s, though nobody has run the rings to prove it. What is measured is its girth, about four metres around, matched almost exactly by a second trunk growing beside it, close enough that Italy's citizen tree registry logs them as a twinned pair rather than argue over which is which. Both stand in the Lecceta, a stretch of holm oak forest between the old citrus house, now a museum holding a de Chirico and Warhol collection, and the Muro Torto, the Aurelian era wall that has marked this edge of Rome since the third century. Villa Borghese holds roughly 350 trees and only a fraction have any official monumental status; a 2024 letter from the conservation group Amici di Villa Borghese named this hackberry as one of about 30 still waiting on the paperwork that would protect it. No source gives it exact coordinates, only a location inside the wood, so finding it means wandering the Lecceta rather than following a pin. That is true of most of Villa Borghese's older trees: the park has outlived several rounds of formal cataloguing without ever finishing one.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Roughly 10-15 min walk from Spagna or Flaminio metro (Line A), inside Villa Borghese
trees.notes: Two adjacent RAMI register entries (#9251, #9252, both ~430cm girth) folded into one entry as a twinned pair. No coordinates in any source; pin geocoded to the Museo Carlo Bilotti / Aranciera building both sources place the tree near. The 1600s age is the conservation group's own framing, not a scientific dating.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Piazza Perin del Vaga

location.address: Piazza Perin del Vaga, Della Vittoria/Flaminio district
location.neighbourhood: Della Vittoria (RAMI's own field note says quartiere Flaminio; the piazza sits on the boundary, so give both if the writer wants to hedge)

trees.story:
The children who climbed this holm oak gave it its name. From the top they would shout "Anvedi da quassù se vede tutta Roma", Roman dialect for look, from up here you can see the whole of Rome, and the tree has been Tutta Roma ever since. They were doing it around 1919, so the oak was already climbable then; the register's own reckoning puts its planting at about 1900.

That shout is now on file. When Italy added the tree to its national list of monumental trees in 2025, the criteria included historical and cultural value alongside form and bearing, which is unusual in Rome, where most entries are listed for size alone. And this is not a giant: 2.80 metres around the trunk, 18 metres tall, measured in November 2025 and found in good health.

It stands in Piazza Perin del Vaga, a residential square in Della Vittoria on the edge of Flaminio, north of the centre near the Tiber and a fair way from anything a visitor would otherwise be walking to. Which is more or less the point of it. Nobody built a monument here. A tree went into the ground around the turn of the last century, a generation of local children went up it, one of them said something worth repeating, and a hundred years later the Italian state wrote it down.
verified_sources: MASAF national register / Lazio regional register, sheet 63/H501/RM/12 (girth 280 cm, height 18 m, criteria: form and bearing; historical, cultural or religious value)

https://ilregistrodeglialberi.it/17724-tutta-roma-leccio-roma-rm-lazio (RAMI entry #17724, AMI code 63/H501/RM/12 matches the register sheet exactly; coordinates 41.925194,12.464699 match to the metre; girth 2.80 m and height 18.00 m match; registered 17/11/2025; health 'Buona'; accessibility 'Accessibile'; estimated age ~126 years calculated from the registered birth year, i.e. planted around 1900)
trees.access: Free, public piazza, no restrictions
trees.transport: In the residential Della Vittoria/Flaminio district, roughly 15-20 minutes' walk from Piazzale Flaminio or Lepanto (Metro A)

trees.name: The Hackberry of the Parco degli Scipioni

location.address: Parco degli Scipioni, Via di Porta Latina 16
location.neighbourhood: Via Appia / Porta Latina, near the Aurelian Walls

trees.story:
Two official surveys measured this hackberry and agreed on its waist to within a centimetre: four metres around. They do not agree on its height. Italy's national monumental tree register records 20 metres. The Appia Antica park authority, in its own catalogue of notable trees, says 15. Both figures are current, neither has been withdrawn, and there is no way from here to tell which tape was right, so take the tree as somewhere between the two.

It is about a hundred years old, which makes it younger than nearly everything around it. The Parco degli Scipioni is laid out over the tomb of the Scipios, burial vault of the family that produced the general who beat Hannibal, with the columbarium of Pomponius Hylas a few steps away and the Aurelian Walls along the edge. The park in its present form is the work of Raffaele de Vico, who designed it around 1929, and this hackberry went in as part of that design: a piece of 20th century landscaping now the largest living thing in a park built on third century BC ground.

The park authority calls it one of its most important specimens, for its size, its bearing and the balance of its crown, and rates its health as good.

A second hackberry, slightly stouter, stands about a hundred metres off against the Aurelian wall itself. It is on the register too. So far nobody else has written it down.
verified_sources: MASAF national register / Lazio regional register, sheet 66/H501/RM/12 (girth 401 cm, height 20 m)

https://www.parcoappiaantica.it/il-territorio/alberi-di-pregio-appia-antica/ (Parco Regionale dell'Appia Antica's own 'alberi di pregio' catalogue: Parco degli Scipioni, Via di Porta Latina 16, height 15 m, circumference 400 cm, estimated age ~100 years, stato fitosanitario Buono; described as integrated into Raffaele de Vico's 1931 landscape design and as one of the park's most important specimens for its dimensions, bearing and balanced canopy)
trees.access: Free, public park within the Parco Regionale dell'Appia Antica, standard park hours (roughly 7am to sunset)
trees.transport: Entrance at Via di Porta Latina 16, near Porta Latina in the Aurelian Walls; roughly 20-25 minutes' walk from Circo Massimo (Metro B), or reachable by bus along Via Appia Antica
